source_neutral.procedure: Compare the internal sequences of separate procurement record series to determine their relative chronological positions and assess whether accounts of steering toward a preferred bidder are compatible with the resulting sequence. Candidate series are successive tender or specification versions, scoring sheets and revisions, email threads, public register entries, and interview accounts of event order. Each series is treated as one unit containing ordered items: version changes, messages, register entries, score revisions, or recalled events. Procurement events expected to appear in several series include publication, clarification rounds, deadline changes, bid receipt, evaluation sessions, and the award notice. An item's calendar position is uncertain when its date is absent, supported solely by its stated date or editable metadata, or based on recollection. Potential anomalies include an absent item, an item present where none is expected, or a date inconsistent with the item's content. The process establishes internal order, constructs a reference chronology from independently dated records, selects distinctive events before comparing chronological placements, tests placements across independent series, and compares placements implied by the official timeline, an innocent explanation, and the steering hypothesis. The packet does not establish which records exist; applicability is conditional.
source_neutral.action: 1. Inventory each series, recording provenance and authentication status. Count series derived from one another as one evidential unit, including forwarded copies, summaries compiled from emails, and interview accounts refreshed from documents. 2. Establish item order within each series using internal evidence alone: version numbering, tracked changes, quoted text in reply chains, sequential reference numbers, and content presupposing earlier content. Record stated dates without relying on them at this stage. 3. Construct the reference chronology from items whose dating does not depend on the parties under scrutiny, such as public register entries, published notices, and copies held and time-stamped by third parties. Check these dated items against one another before using them as the reference. 4. Before attempting any chronological alignment, record the distinctive, non-routine events expected in more than one series, such as a changed eligibility threshold, a reweighted criterion, a moved deadline, or unusual wording. Exclude routine recurring items, including boilerplate edits and regular meetings, from the selected comparison features. 5. Compare each series whose chronological position is uncertain with the reference chronology, varying its relative position. At each candidate placement, check correspondence in the order and relative spacing of the preselected features. Repeat the comparison against every other independent series. 6. When a placement fits except at one point, state a specific hypothesis of a missing item, an extra item, or a misassigned date, and test it against the other series. Do not accept it based on the series in which it was identified alone. 7. Attempt placements implied by the official timeline and at least one innocent explanation alongside the placement implied by the steering hypothesis. Record which placements remain compatible with the comparisons.
source_neutral.observables: The specified success signal is one relative placement at which several preselected features correspond in the same order and relative spacing across two or more independent series, while alternative placements fail to match at least some features. At that placement, inconsistencies can be assigned to specific positions. Possible observations, not findings supplied by the packet, include a version referenced in emails but absent from the tender file; a scoring sheet whose criteria correspond to a specification version placed later than the sheet's stated date; bidder material reflecting a requirement at a position before its independently dated publication; or an interview account whose event order matches the documents only if one recalled event is repositioned. A match on a single feature, a match between series with a common origin, a match based on routine repeating items, or a placement selected after the comparisons because it fits the steering hypothesis does not meet the specified signal. Another observable outcome is that the official timeline aligns with all independent series and reveals no anomaly.
source_neutral.inferential_warrant: A consistent alignment across multiple series supports bounded chronological claims: assigning previously undated or doubtfully dated items a position relative to independently dated events; checking the official timeline against independent series and extending the dated account across intervals covered by some series but not others; and stating that a specific item is probably missing, extra, or misdated, while identifying the supporting series. These claims bear on whether requirements or weightings changed before or after contact with a particular bidder, whether criteria or scores changed before or after bid receipt, and whether bidder material reflects a requirement before its independently dated public availability. The procedure establishes sequence and chronological compatibility: which accounts remain possible and which are excluded. A sequence consistent with steering does not prove steering. Alignment does not date purpose or knowledge; these remain matters for corroborating interviews, competing explanations, and disconfirming evidence. Relevant alternative explanations include legitimate clarification rounds, template reuse, incumbent familiarity, and prior market consultation. Report corroborated placements as corroborated facts, anomalies as unresolved gaps, and steering as an allegation unless separately corroborated. Report support for the official timeline as constraining the steering account.
source_neutral.problem_decomposition: The units are procurement record series and the individual items ordered within each series. Internal dependencies establish order within a series; shared distinctive procurement events permit comparisons between series. Independently dated items provide the reference chronology. Series derived from a common origin constitute one evidential unit rather than independent confirmations. Comparisons examine event order and relative spacing across overlapping intervals. A local mismatch is represented as a specific hypothesis about a missing item, an extra item, or an incorrect date, whose support must come from other series. Competing chronological arrangements correspond to the official timeline, at least one innocent explanation, and the steering hypothesis. Chronological position and compatibility are assessed separately from authentication, purpose, knowledge, and corroboration of steering.
source_neutral.next_inquiry: If a single series is available or the series do not overlap, seek further records before starting the procedure. For each unplaced item or hypothesised gap, seek the specific missing record or an independent interview account covering that interval, then repeat steps 5 through 7 with the added material. Purpose and knowledge remain subjects for corroborating interviews, competing explanations, and disconfirming evidence.
source_neutral.limits: Applicability assumes, without establishing as facts, that more than one series can be obtained, that their periods overlap, that at least one series can be dated independently of the parties under scrutiny, and that the procurement includes events distinctive enough to recognise across series. Do not start if a single series is available or no series overlap. Stop attempting to place an item and record it as unplaced if more than one placement fits comparably well, the fit rests on a single feature, the overlap contains too few features, or the fit depends on a series that is not independent. Do not force a placement. Features specific to one series, including an official's drafting habits, system migration, clock or time-zone offsets, and template reuse, can imitate or conceal a comparison feature. Procurement with few distinctive events provides little basis for matching and weakly constrains alignment. Brief email threads, few versions, recurring boilerplate, and periodic meetings may fit several positions and produce false alignments. Transcription errors, text-recognition errors, editable or reset metadata, and errors in interview recollection can affect the comparisons. The independently dated reference chronology may itself be incorrect, amended, or entered late; an error can affect every item positioned against it. Series covering different intervals cannot be positioned against one another, and placement across an uncovered interval is unsupported. Copied or derived records can appear to provide repeated confirmation without independent support. A gap does not prove misconduct: retention practices or incomplete disclosure may explain absent records. Selecting features or placements with the steering hypothesis in mind risks fitting the observations to that conclusion. Alignment constrains order, not intent. Authentication is a separate precondition; aligning unauthenticated records does not authenticate them.
